Secure & Sustainable AI Systems

Understanding the joint costs of intelligence, robustness and resource use across learning and deployment.

Research Description

Overview

We study security and efficiency together, asking how attacks, defenses and learning strategies change predictive utility, energy use and response time. This matters when battery budgets, response deadlines and computing costs limit deployment of on-device AI, LLMs and agentic services across edge and cloud systems.

Existing work examines energy–latency attacks, model-pruning defenses, environmental-cost measurement and robustness–sustainability tradeoffs. Resource-aware agents and data-center-scale evaluation are emerging directions, not established infrastructure deployments.

Research Thrusts

Resource-aware resilience

Measure robustness alongside computational cost, memory, latency and energy rather than optimizing accuracy in isolation.

Efficient learning and deployment

Investigate how model choices and deployment constraints interact in edge and resource-constrained AI systems.

Emerging AI infrastructure

Extend questions about efficiency and security toward agent systems and AI infrastructure. Data-center-scale research remains a proposed direction, not an established deployment.

Research Goals

Measure predictive utility, adversarial resilience, energy and latency together, including resource-constrained settings.

Intellectual Merit

Make security–sustainability tradeoffs explicit and comparable across methods and system conditions.

Research Impact

The intended contribution is evidence for choosing AI designs under practical resource and security constraints. Benefits must be measured for each workload and platform rather than assumed from a smaller model alone.

Current Projects & Emerging Directions

Published and preprint foundations

Resource-aware adversarial resilience

Sensing workload→Attack / defense→Accuracy + energy + latency

Attacks can change more than a prediction: they can also increase the time and energy required to process sensor data. This project examines that broader attack surface and the resource costs introduced by defenses.

Research objectives

Evaluate predictive performance alongside energy and latency, including the tradeoffs created by model pruning.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

The published Sponge Attacks study provides a sensing-AI foundation. Comparisons should account for model, device and workload so that apparent efficiency gains are not confused with reduced utility.

Selected publications

Sponge attacks on sensing ai: Energy-latency vulnerabilities and defense via model pruning ↗

Relevance & Applications

Resource-constrained sensing and edge platforms need dependable response times as well as accurate outputs. These evaluations help identify when a defense shifts costs elsewhere rather than removing them.

Impact

The linked work studies energy–latency vulnerabilities and model-pruning defenses. Its potential benefit is a fuller basis for comparing security costs; this is not a claim of deployed protection or measured real-world savings.

Existing research

Sustainable machine learning

Training & defense→Measure resource use→Explain tradeoffs

Security measures are part of the computational workload of AI. Training, repeated evaluation and adversarial defenses can change energy requirements and their associated environmental costs.

Research objectives

Make resource and environmental measurements transparent and compare the costs of learning and defense under clearly stated assumptions.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

Published work reviews carbon-emission quantification and examines the sustainability and social costs of adversarial training. The approach emphasizes the measurement boundary, hardware and energy assumptions behind an estimate.

Selected publications

Selected sustainability publications ↗

Relevance & Applications

Researchers can use these distinctions to report security–efficiency tradeoffs more responsibly. Estimated carbon costs are not equivalent to measured reductions in operational emissions.

Impact

Published work reviews carbon-emission quantification and examines the costs of adversarial training. The intended benefit is more transparent tradeoff reporting, not a claim of verified emissions reductions in deployed systems.

Emerging direction · not an established deployment

AI infrastructure and agent systems

Devices & agents→Edge / cloud coordination→Security + resource budgets

As AI workloads move between devices, edge services and larger infrastructure, security and resource decisions become interconnected. Agent workflows introduce additional questions about the information and computation passed between components.

Research objectives

Develop an evaluation agenda for trustworthy coordination, resource allocation and evidence flow across connected AI systems.

Approach & Intellectual Merit

This is a proposed systems direction informed by existing efficiency and security research. Data-center-scale evaluation is a future target; no dedicated infrastructure deployment or project-specific performance result is asserted.

Relevance & Applications

The long-term relevance is to resource-aware AI services whose security cannot be assessed at the model level alone. Operational impact will require system-scale experiments and independent validation.

Impact

The intended impact is a framework for studying how security, resource constraints, and evidence flow interact at system scale. This remains an emerging agenda; no project-specific outcomes, infrastructure deployment, or operational savings are claimed.
